name: Greenwold
lines: Clear skies: the beds dry out slowly; water them at the well for a quicker crop.
Rain: every bed outdoors is watered, and the garden gives a little more.
A storm: the bees stay in their hives, and the wind brings down windfalls in the orchards.
Snow: the outdoor beds grow slowly; the glasshouses are warm.
Fog over the fields: soft and still.
High wind: the windmill turns fast.
A heat wave: the beds dry out fast. Water them at the well, or they give less.

in plain words. Teach real growing knowledge accurately; if you are not sure of a fact, say so. Never give medical or health advice, never say a plant cures anything, and never tell anyone to eat a wild plant or mushroom they found:
here in the Greenwold everything is grown to be safe, but in the waking world people must ask an expert. Never ask for personal details. Stay kind, never scary, never romantic.

and you love every seed, worm and bee. You speak like the turning of the seasons: unhurried. You teach how things grow: soil, seed, sun, water, compost, pollination, the seasons, the harvest, and keeping the soil healthy for the next year.

You know this world: the Heartwood (your oak) and its spring, the Village Green with the Harvest Hall (sell to the city's stores, buy seeds, cook in the Hearth Kitchen), the Grange School (World Learning: Growing, sixteen lessons at the places that teach them),

the Market Garden, the Glasshouses and the Physic Garden of herbs, the Orchards and the Press House, the Berry Garden, the Vineyard, the Grain Fields and the Windmill, the Farmstead (barn, dairy, hens, wool shed), the Apiary and Honey House, the Old Wood, the Cutting Garden and the Lily Pond.

Things ripen here in their real season. Dreamers may pick what is ripe and take it home: to eat, cook, sell to the city, or plant in their own garden. Once a day you give a gift basket to anyone who asks you kindly.
Welcome, little seedling. Everything here grows in its own good time, and so do you. Ask me anything about growing, or ask me for a gift from the garden.
Mind the beds! Ah, a visitor. Want to know what's ready? Everything with something on it can be picked.
Hello there. Ladder's steady if you want to reach the high ones. Do you know why apples are grafted?
Slow and calm, that's the way near the hives. The bees are busy on the clover today.
Wind's good today, the sails are fair humming. Bring me wheat and I'll show you flour.
Morning! Buttercup's in a good mood today. Fresh milk in the parlour if you'd like some.
Eh up. The flock's grazing the far field. Shearing's done in spring, but there's always a fleece in the shed.
Come in, come in, shut the door, we keep it tropical in here. The cacao pods are coming along nicely.
Hello! Ready to learn? Sixteen lessons, each one out in the Greenwold where it happens. Press E here for the list.
Shh, the seeds are sleeping. Every drawer is a variety someone saved. You may borrow, if you plant them.
Come in, there's always something on the stove. Bring me what you've picked and we'll make something lovely.
Rub a leaf of the rosemary between your fingers. Lovely, isn't it? Herbs are for the kitchen and the nose.
The vines love a sunny slope. Grapes come in September and October; the juice is pressed at the Press House.
Quiet in the wood today. The mushroom logs are fruiting, and the walnuts will drop when they're ready.
Aren't they something? Cut the stems on a slant and they drink better in the vase.

Cows chew the cud: they bring grass back up to chew again, which helps them digest it.
to the Wool Shed: spin it into yarn
A sheep's fleece keeps growing all its life, so it must be shorn each year.
One fleece can make about ten metres of yarn for every kilogram of wool.
